932.title: Padmasambhava
932.hook: the tradition tells how Guru Rinpoche tamed the forces blocking the teaching in Tibet
932.howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhists, especially in the Nyingma school, recite Padmasambhava's mantra, keep his image on their shrines, and hold feast days in his honor.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shantarakshita, the abbot, was invited, and when trouble came he named another teacher. Your line was the invitation. Whom did you ask? Day nine hundred thirty-two.

In Tibetan paintings he sits in layered robes, a lotus hat topped with a feather, a staff resting in the crook of his arm, a vajra in his hand, his eyes wide open. Tibetans call him Guru Rinpoche, the precious teacher. The abbot from India named him. The king sent for him. And according to the story, on his way in, the land itself rose up to stop him. Today: Padmasambhava.
screen: `A LOTUS HAT, A STAFF, WIDE EYES.` → `GURU RINPOCHE.` → `THE LAND RISES AGAINST HIM.`

segments.voice: His name is Sanskrit: Padmasambhava, born from a lotus. Tradition tells the story behind the name: he appeared as a child sitting in a lotus on a lake in the land of Oddiyana. He's a tantric master, a yogi of power rather than an abbot of rules, which is exactly why the abbot named him. On his road into Tibet, the stories say, the spirits of the mountains, lakes and passes rose up to block him with storms, landslides and sickness. And here's the surprising turn. He didn't destroy them. He tamed them. One after another, the accounts say, he subdued these forces and bound them by oath to protect the teaching. The very powers that blocked the road became its guardians. Tibetan temples honor protectors who, in the story, began as its enemies. So the word tamed is precise. Taming isn't killing. A tamed horse still has all its strength. It just stops throwing the rider. Some Tibetan teachers read this story in two ways at once, without asking anyone to choose. Outwardly, it's the history of how the teaching settled into a land that already had its own spirits. Inwardly, it's a map of the mind. Anger, fear and pride rise up against practice. In this reading they needn't be wiped out. They can be brought under oath, and their energy turned toward the path. The Nyingma, the old school of Tibetan Buddhism, looks to Padmasambhava as its founder.
screen: `BORN FROM A LOTUS.` · `THE SPIRITS BLOCK THE ROAD.` · `TAMED, NOT DESTROYED.` · `OUTWARD HISTORY, INWARD MAP.` · then, large: `THE OBSTACLES TAMED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: tame one obstacle. Settle, and breathe. Name one thing that's blocking your road right now: a worry, an irritation, a habit. Don't fight it. Let it come into view, and notice where it sits in the body. Then ask it, quietly, what its strength could be for. Worry might become care. Anger might become courage for what's right. Stay with that for a few breaths. If it won't be tamed today, that's fine: let it be there, and simply keep breathing. The bell holds the time.
Padmasambhava. Born from a lotus. Guru Rinpoche, who, tradition says, tamed the forces blocking the teaching in Tibet and made them its guardians. Today's word.
Your line: the obstacles tamed. Today, when something blocks you, try taming before fighting: ask what its strength could be for. Day nine hundred thirty-two.

933.title: Samye
933.hook: the first monastery in Tibet, laid out as a mandala
933.howItsDone: Pilgrims to Samye walk clockwise around the monastery and its central temple, and Tibetan Buddhists make mandalas in paint and colored sand as supports for meditation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Padmasambhava, born from a lotus, who tamed the forces blocking the way. Your line was the obstacles tamed. What did you try taming instead of fighting? Day nine hundred thirty-three.

A story tells that when the king asked what his monastery would look like, Padmasambhava showed it to him, whole, in the palm of his hand. The king looked, and all he could say was: inconceivable! In Tibetan, samye. And that, the story goes, became the monastery's name. Whether that's heard as history or as a beautiful way of saying it, the place itself is laid out like nothing else around it. Seen from above, it looks like a diagram. Today: Samye.
screen: `A MONASTERY IN A PALM.` → `INCONCEIVABLE.` → `FROM ABOVE, A DIAGRAM.`

segments.voice: Tibetan histories remember Samye as the first monastery in Tibet, raised under King Trisong Detsen with the abbot Shantarakshita and Padmasambhava. What makes it unusual is its plan. Samye was laid out as a mandala, a map of the universe as Buddhists in India pictured it. At the center rises the main temple. It stands for Mount Meru, the great mountain at the middle of the world. Around it, smaller temples stand for the continents in each direction, with lesser shrines beside them. And around everything runs a round wall, the ring of mountains at the world's edge. So walking into Samye is walking into a picture of the cosmos, from the rim toward the center. A mandala may be familiar as a painting, or as a design laid out in colored sand. Samye makes it a place. Pilgrims walk around it, the way they walk around temples, keeping the center on their right. Each circuit draws them around the middle, never straight at it. And here's what the plan says without a word. The center isn't alone, and the edge isn't outside. Everything, from the farthest wall to the middle shrine, belongs to one design. The histories add that the first Tibetan monks were ordained here, by the Indian abbot. So a story that began with an invitation now has a home: a building that teaches by its shape.
screen: `THE FIRST MONASTERY, THE HISTORIES SAY.` · `MOUNT MERU AT THE CENTER.` · `CONTINENTS, AND A ROUND WALL.` · `A BUILDING THAT TEACHES BY SHAPE.` · then, large: `A MONASTERY AS A MANDALA.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: picture a mandala as a place. Settle, and close your eyes if that's comfortable. Imagine standing outside a round wall. Step through the gate. Walk slowly around the inside, keeping the center on your right, and with each circuit come a little closer. Pass the smaller temples as you go. At last, stand before the temple at the center, and simply rest there with the breath. There's nothing to do at the center but arrive. The bell holds the time.
Samye. Inconceivable, the story says. Tibet's first monastery in the histories, laid out as a mandala, a map of the world you can walk around. Today's word.
Your line: a monastery as a mandala. Today, find the center of one room you're in, and walk once around it, slowly, before you sit down. Day nine hundred thirty-three.

934.title: The debate
934.hook: the Samye debate: Kamalashila's gradual path against a Chan teacher's sudden path, as the Tibetan accounts tell it
934.howItsDone: Debate is part of training in Tibetan monasteries, where monks question each other in courtyards with set gestures and a clap of the hands, and students study Kamalashila's Stages of Meditation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Samye, the monastery laid out as a mandala. Your line was a monastery as a mandala. Did you walk once around a center? Day nine hundred thirty-four.

Two teachers in Tibet were saying different things about how awakening happens, and the king had to decide which way his monasteries would go. One, a Chan master from China, taught that awakening is sudden: stop grasping at thoughts and see your own nature directly. The other, Kamalashila, an Indian scholar and a student of the abbot Shantarakshita, taught that it comes step by step: ethics, study, careful reflection, meditation. So, as the Tibetan accounts tell it, the king called them to debate. Today: the debate.
screen: `TWO TEACHERS, TWO PATHS.` → `SUDDEN, OR STEP BY STEP?` → `THE KING CALLS A DEBATE.`

segments.voice: Tibetans remember the Chinese master as Hashang Mahayana. In the accounts, he argues that any thought, good or bad, clouds the mind's clear nature, the way white clouds and black clouds alike hide the sun. So stop chasing thoughts, stop grasping, and the sun is already there. Kamalashila answers: if you stop all thinking, how will you ever see clearly? Wisdom needs careful reflection. Not-thinking alone is only a blank. He lays out stages, each resting on the one before, and tradition says he wrote them down in his Stages of Meditation. In the Tibetan accounts, Kamalashila wins, and the king rules that Tibet will follow the gradual path of the Indian teachers. But be careful with the scoreboard. This version of the story comes to us from one side. Other records, from the Chinese side, tell it differently, and historians ask whether it was a single debate at all or a longer exchange. And the sudden teaching didn't vanish. You met it in Korea earlier on this road, when Chinul said awaken suddenly, then cultivate gradually. Chan and Zen schools carry the sudden way still, and Tibetan traditions later taught their own direct ways of looking at the nature of mind. So one fair way to hear the debate is as two real insights pressing against each other. Sudden: the sun was never gone. Gradual: the clouds still need clearing. Gradual and sudden.
screen: `WHITE CLOUDS, BLACK CLOUDS.` · `NOT-THINKING ALONE IS A BLANK.` · `ONE SIDE TELLS THIS STORY.` · `TWO INSIGHTS, PRESSING.` · then, large: `GRADUAL AND SUDDEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hear both sides. Settle, and breathe. For the first half of the sit, try the sudden way: let every thought, pleasant or not, pass without grabbing it, like clouds crossing the sky. For the second half, try the gradual way: choose one thought, about kindness or about change, and turn it over carefully. Notice what each is like from the inside, without deciding which is right. The bell holds the time.
The debate. At Samye, as the Tibetan accounts tell it, Kamalashila's gradual path met a Chan master's sudden path, and the king chose. Today's word.
Your line: gradual and sudden. Today, when you disagree with someone, state their side as well as they would before you give yours. Day nine hundred thirty-four.

935.title: The dark years
935.hook: after King Langdarma, monasteries were closed and the teaching went quiet
935.howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhists tell the story of the dark years as a lesson in endurance, and the Nyingma tradition honors treasure revealers who bring to light teachings said to have been hidden by Padmasambhava.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the debate at Samye: sudden awakening against step by step. Your line was gradual and sudden. Whose side did you state fairly? Day nine hundred thirty-five.

A few monks lead pack animals east, away from central Tibet. In the loads are books of the monastic rules. Behind them, the Tibetan histories say, King Langdarma has turned against the monasteries, and the halls that earlier kings built and filled are emptying. The monks aren't carrying gold. They're carrying the rules for how a monk is made, so that one day it can be done again. And the question rides with them: what keeps a practice alive when there's nowhere left to practice it in the open? Today: terma.
screen: `MONKS HEAD EAST.` → `THE RULES IN THEIR PACKS.` → `WHAT KEEPS A PRACTICE ALIVE?`

segments.voice: The histories tell it sharply. Langdarma turns against the monasteries, and the royal support they lived on is cut off. His reign ends violently, and after it the old empire breaks apart among rival lords. For a long stretch there is no king to invite an abbot and no royal temple to pay for. Historians today ask whether Langdarma was as fierce as the later accounts say, or whether the loss of royal money did much of the damage on its own. Either way, the great monasteries went dark. But quiet isn't the same as gone. The stories remember three kinds of keepers. First, a few monks who fled to the far east of Tibet carrying the monastic rules, so that the line of ordination could one day be handed on again. Second, lay practitioners, married men and women in villages, who kept chanting and meditating at home, out of sight. Third, the texts themselves: scrolls hidden away and, in the Nyingma telling, teachings Padmasambhava had concealed to be found when the time was right. Those hidden teachings are called terma, treasures. That's what a hard time looks like from inside a tradition. Mostly not a grand stand. A rule remembered. A chant said low in a kitchen. A scroll wrapped and set aside. Small things kept going, because nobody knew when the doors would open again.
screen: `THE MONASTERIES GO DARK.` · `MONKS CARRY THE RULES EAST.` · `VILLAGERS KEEP IT AT HOME.` · `TEXTS HIDDEN AS TREASURES.` · then, large: `IT WENT QUIET.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep one practice through hard times. Settle, and breathe. Choose one small thing you could do even on your worst day: a few slow breaths, a line you say, one kind act, a moment of thanks. Make it small enough that nothing could stop you. Then do it now, quietly, as if no one would ever know. Let the rest of the sit be that one practice, kept. The bell holds the time.
Terma. Hidden treasures, texts and teachings concealed to be found later, kept safe through Tibet's dark years after King Langdarma. Today's word.
Your line: it went quiet. Today, do your one small practice once, even if the day is easy, so it's ready when the day isn't. Day nine hundred thirty-five.

936.title: Atisha comes
936.hook: the Indian master Atisha arrives and renews the teaching
936.howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhists study Atisha's Lamp for the Path and the stages-of-the-path teachings built on it, and practice mind training, which traces its lineage to Atisha.

segments.voice: Yesterday, terma, hidden through the dark years when the monasteries closed and the teaching went quiet. Your line was it went quiet. What small practice did you keep? Day nine hundred thirty-six.

In the far west of Tibet, a royal family wanted the teaching back, and done properly. Tibetans tell a story about one of these kings, Yeshe O. Tradition says he was captured by an enemy while gathering gold to invite a great teacher from India. When his family raised his ransom, he sent word back: don't spend it on me. Use it to bring the teacher. He died in captivity, the story says, and the invitation went on without him. Today: Atisha comes.
screen: `A KING GATHERS GOLD.` → `DON'T SPEND IT ON ME.` → `THE INVITATION GOES ON.`

segments.voice: The teacher was Atisha, an Indian master from the monastery of Vikramashila. Tradition says he was reluctant, and that his own abbot didn't want to let him go. But he came over the mountains, and he stayed in Tibet for the rest of his life. What he found, the accounts say, was a teaching that had scattered. Some people kept the rules and looked down on meditation. Others claimed secret practices and let ethics slide. So Atisha wrote a short text for the Tibetans: A Lamp for the Path to Enlightenment. Its gift is order. It sorts practitioners by what they're aiming for. Some aim for a better life to come. Some aim for their own freedom. Some aim to free all beings. And the path rises in stages, each resting on the one before: ethics, then meditation, then wisdom, with compassion running through all of it. Nothing thrown away. Everything in its place. Atisha also taught ways of training the mind: turning everyday trouble into practice, and putting others before yourself. His student Dromtonpa gathered his followers into the Kadam school, and later Tibetan schools built on his Lamp. So this is what renewal looked like. Not a new religion, and not a return to exactly what was lost. A teacher who came in, listened, saw what had scattered, and lit a lamp so the pieces could be found again.
screen: `ATISHA LEAVES VIKRAMASHILA.` · `THE TEACHING HAD SCATTERED.` · `A LAMP FOR THE PATH.` · `EACH STAGE RESTS ON THE LAST.` · then, large: `THE RENEWAL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: welcome a renewal. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something in your life that once mattered and has scattered: a habit, a friendship, a practice, a hope. No scolding. Just picture lighting one small lamp beside it, enough to see where the pieces are. Ask what one first step back would look like. Then rest with the breath, steady as a small flame. The bell holds the time.
Atisha comes. The Indian master Atisha arrives in Tibet and renews the teaching, putting the path back in order with his Lamp. Today's word.
Your line: the renewal. Today, take one first step back toward something good that scattered, and let that one step be enough. Day nine hundred thirty-six.

937.title: The translator
937.hook: Rinchen Zangpo, who traveled to India to bring back texts
937.carry: knowing the words, and living them
937.howItsDone: In Tibetan Buddhism, the great translators, the lotsawas, are remembered by name and honored as teachers, and Tibetan translations of Indian texts traditionally name the Indian scholar and the Tibetan translator who made them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Atisha came over the mountains from India, and the teaching in Tibet came back to life. Your line was the renewal. What did you let begin again? Day nine hundred thirty-seven.

A young man from western Tibet sets out on foot, heading west, over passes where the snow never quite leaves. He doesn't speak the language of the people he's going to. He doesn't have the books he's going for. What he has is a question: what did the Buddha actually say, and what did the great teachers of India write about it? The only way to find out is to go, learn their language, and carry the answers home on his back. His name was Rinchen Zangpo. Today, the translator.
screen: `A YOUNG MAN ON FOOT.` → `NO LANGUAGE, NO BOOKS.` → `GO, LEARN, CARRY IT HOME.`

segments.voice: First, the journey. Tradition says Rinchen Zangpo was sent from western Tibet, where kings had begun calling the teaching back after the quiet years. He went to Kashmir and northern India, studied Sanskrit, and sat with Indian teachers until he could read their books the way they read them. Then he came home with texts, and with teachers willing to come too. Second, the work itself. A Tibetan translation was often not one person alone at a desk. An Indian scholar, a pandita, and a Tibetan translator worked side by side: one knew the Sanskrit from the inside, the other knew how Tibetans would hear it. Tibetans call a translator a lotsawa, and it became a title of honor. Rinchen Zangpo is remembered as the great translator. Third, why translation is so hard here. A Buddhist word carries a whole teaching inside it. Get the word for emptiness slightly wrong, and a reader walks off in the wrong direction for years. So the lotsawas tried to choose one Tibetan word for one Sanskrit word and keep to it, so that a reader in a far valley would meet the same teaching a reader near the capital did. Fourth, a story about meeting. Yesterday's teacher, Atisha, arrived when Rinchen Zangpo was already old and famous. A story is told that Atisha questioned him and found his learning enormous. Then Atisha asked how he put all of it into practice, at once, on the cushion. The old translator, the story goes, went quiet, and then went into retreat. Knowing the words, and living them, are two different journeys. He had made the first one already. The story says he began the second.
screen: `THE ROAD TO KASHMIR AND INDIA.` · `A PANDITA AND A LOTSAWA, SIDE BY SIDE.` · `ONE WORD FOR ONE WORD.` · `KNOWING THE WORDS, LIVING THEM.` · then, large: `THE TRANSLATOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn a word in another language. Pick one word that matters to you, maybe kindness, or patience, or home. If you know it in another language, a grandparent's, a neighbor's, one from school, bring that word to mind. If you don't, take lotsawa, translator. Settle, and breathe. On each out-breath, say the word silently. Notice that it's more than a sound: someone had to carry it across a border so you could hear it. Then let the word go and rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
The translator. A lotsawa like Rinchen Zangpo, who walked to India and brought the teaching back into Tibetan, one careful word at a time. Today's word.
Your line: knowing the words, and living them. Today, be one for somebody: explain one thing in words they actually use, a form, a recipe, a piece of news. Day nine hundred thirty-seven.

938.title: Two canons
938.hook: the Kangyur, the Buddha's words, and the Tengyur, the commentaries
938.howItsDone: Tibetan monasteries keep the Kangyur and the Tengyur on their shelves, and in some communities the Kangyur is carried in procession or read aloud in full as an act of devotion; the Tengyur's commentaries are the core of monastic study.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the translator: Rinchen Zangpo walked to India and carried the teaching home, one careful word at a time. Your line was knowing the words, and living them. Who did you translate something for? Day nine hundred thirty-eight.

Long wooden shelves in a Tibetan temple, and on them, row after row of long narrow books wrapped in cloth, each one pressed between two boards. They don't look like books on a bookstore shelf. They're loose pages, wider than they are tall, stacked and tied. Many of those pages passed through the hands of translators like yesterday's. And if you could read the labels, you'd find the shelves fall into two great collections. Today, two canons.
screen: `LONG BOOKS WRAPPED IN CLOTH.` → `LOOSE PAGES BETWEEN BOARDS.` → `TWO GREAT COLLECTIONS.`

segments.voice: First, the Kangyur. The name is usually explained as the translated word: the teachings Tibetans hold to be the Buddha's own, his sutras, his rules for monks and nuns, and the tantras, all turned from Indian languages into Tibetan. This is the voice of the teacher himself, as Tibetans receive it. Second, the Tengyur, usually explained as the translated treatises. These are the commentaries: the great Indian teachers explaining, arguing, organizing, and teaching how to practice what the Buddha said. Nagarjuna on emptiness is here. Shantideva's guide to the bodhisattva's way of life is here. Logic, medicine, grammar and poetry are here too, because Indian scholars studied all of them. Third, why keep them apart. Putting the words in one collection and the commentaries in another is a kind of honesty. A reader always knows whether they're hearing the Buddha, as tradition receives him, or a later teacher doing their best to explain. The commentaries are honored, studied and memorized. But they stand on a different shelf. Fourth, why it matters on an ordinary day. Much of what we hear arrives already mixed: what someone said, and what somebody else says it means. A headline, a quote passed around, a family story. The two canons are a quiet habit worth borrowing: keep the words and the commentary on separate shelves, and know which one you're holding. And a look back at the week. Padmasambhava tamed the obstacles. Samye was built as a mandala. A debate weighed gradual and sudden. Then the dark years, when it went quiet. Atisha brought the renewal. The translator carried the words. Today, those words find their shelves.
screen: `THE KANGYUR: THE TRANSLATED WORD.` · `THE TENGYUR: THE TRANSLATED TREATISES.` · `KEPT APART, ON PURPOSE.` · `KNOW WHICH ONE YOU'RE HOLDING.` · then, large: `WORDS AND COMMENTARIES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name the two collections. Settle, and breathe. On an out-breath, say silently: Kangyur, the Buddha's words. Breathe. On the next, say: Tengyur, the commentaries. Go back and forth a few times, slowly, until the two names sit easily. Then let the names rest, and simply listen: to the room, to the breath, to whatever is here before anyone explains it. The bell holds the time.
